title: How Marriage Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explain how marriage works: its legal nature as a contract with federal benefits, state-by-state licensing rules, and the marriage age trend. They cover same-sex marriage laws and the Supreme Court cases on DOMA, alternatives like civil unions, domestic partnerships and reciprocal beneficiary relationships, common law marriage, cohabitation trends, research on what predicts marriage success and divorce (including the seven year itch), and the difference between dates from the perspectives of men and women. The episode closes with a listener mail segment.

segments.title: Opening and framing marriage
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the episode on marriage, note it will touch on same-sex marriage because it is in the news, and describe marriage as a legal contract that confers legal rights.

segments.title: Marriage license and state laws
segments.summary: The application and license process is covered, with marriage age rules varying by state, including minors needing parental consent or court permission, and out-of-state weddings in Las Vegas. Blood tests and officiant requirements are also mentioned.

segments.title: Federal benefits of marriage
segments.summary: Federal legal benefits of being married are described, including hospital visitation, medical decisions, inheritance, insurance, tax filing, Social Security and Medicare, and immigration of a spouse.

segments.title: Health and family benefits of marriage studies
segments.summary: Studies are cited suggesting happily married people live longer and that married-parent households tend to produce stable, well-adjusted kids who do better in school.

segments.title: Median marriage age trends
segments.summary: The hosts discuss rising median age of marriage, citing figures of 28.6 for men and 26.6 for women in the most recent year, and a historical low in the 1950s and 1960s after higher ages in 1890.

segments.title: Polygamy and alternative unions
segments.summary: Plural marriage is mentioned, with a reference to the polygamy episode and the Mormon Church condemnation, with an estimated 30 to 60 thousand practitioners. Civil unions and domestic partnerships are introduced.

segments.title: States and countries recognizing same-sex unions
segments.summary: Nine states allow civil unions for same-sex couples, and a case before the Supreme Court involving a domestic partnership and federal inheritance tax is noted. Full same-sex marriage is available in ten US jurisdictions as of December 2012, while thirty-eight states ban it. Eleven countries are listed as allowing same-sex marriage.

segments.title: DOMA and Bill Clinton's statements
segments.summary: The Defense of Marriage Act is described as defining marriage federally as a union of one man and one woman. Clinton's shifting explanations for signing it in 1996, 2008 and 2009 are recounted, and the states' rights question before the Supreme Court is discussed.

segments.title: Reciprocal beneficiary relationships and civil rights comparison
segments.summary: Hawaii's reciprocal beneficiary relationship is explained as granting some marital rights without making a couple in the eyes of law. Hosts compare the same-sex marriage debate to earlier civil rights struggles.

segments.title: Common law marriage
segments.summary: Common law marriage is explained, including its origins and the myth of a seven-year requirement. Presenting as married (name change, joint taxes) is described, and the fact that only some states recognize it, with Georgia grandfathering some pre-1997 unions, is noted.

segments.title: Cohabitation, divorce rates and predictors of lasting marriage
segments.summary: Trends in cohabitation and the divorce rate are discussed. Studies cited include first-marriage survival rates at twenty years, higher survival for college-educated women, effects of children and shared drinking or fun, religion, and shared curiosity.

segments.title: Seven year itch and dating expectations
segments.summary: The seven-year itch is discussed, with the median US divorce around seven years and Helen Fisher's evolutionary explanation. Hosts also discuss differing expectations of dates between men and women from a University of Denver study.

segments.title: Outro
segments.summary: Hosts sign off and point listeners to the website for more on marriage and other topics.
